## Паттерн 1 — AND-scope (тип A3a)

НАЙДИ в запросе структуру: "[Тип A] and [Тип B] (with|who|which|that|where|serving) [условие]"
Неоднозначность: условие относится к обоим типам или только к последнему?

ОБРАТИ ВНИМАНИЕ: паттерн требует ДВА РАЗНЫХ ТИПА объектов через and, после которых
идёт ограничительный клауз. Числа, даты и одиночные типы паттерн НЕ образуют.

Примеры → is_ambiguous=true:
- "List all banquet halls and conference rooms with a 200 person capacity."
  СТРУКТУРА: [banquet halls] and [conference rooms] WITH [a 200 person capacity]
  ВОПРОС: with 200 — к halls тоже или только к rooms?

- "Give me restaurants and cafes that serve Italian cuisine."
  СТРУКТУРА: [restaurants] and [cafes] THAT [serve Italian cuisine]
  ВОПРОС: that serve — к restaurants тоже или только к cafes?

- "Show me chefs and servers who speak English."
  СТРУКТУРА: [chefs] and [servers] WHO [speak English]
  ВОПРОС: who speak — к chefs тоже или только к servers?

Примеры → is_ambiguous=false:
- "Show all banquet halls and conference rooms where either can hold 200 people."
  ПРИЧИНА: "either" после where = явная дизъюнкция, неоднозначности нет.

- "List all restaurants and also list cafes that serve Italian cuisine."
  ПРИЧИНА: "also list" / "also provide" разбивает перечисление явно, это два раздельных запроса.

- "Provide a list of all chefs and also provide a list of servers who speak English."
  ПРИЧИНА: "also provide a list of" = явное разделение на два отдельных запроса.

- "Which chefs speak English and which servers speak the same language?"
  ПРИЧИНА: "which X [глагол] and which Y [глагол]" = два параллельных полных предложения,
  каждая часть имеет своё подлежащее и глагол. Ограничительного клауза нет.

- "What restaurants serve Italian cuisine and what cafes serve the same cuisine?"
  ПРИЧИНА: "what X [глагол] and what Y [глагол]" = параллельная структура двух вопросов.

- "How many schools have avg math > 560 and are directly funded?"
  ПРИЧИНА: один тип объектов (schools), два условия — нет двух типов.

- "Please provide a list of clients who were born between 1983 and 1987 and whose..."
  ПРИЧИНА: "between 1983 and 1987" — числовой диапазон, не два типа объектов.

---

## Паттерн 2 — Every/Each (тип A3b)

НАЙДИ в запросе "every" или "each" в позиции универсального квантора над множеством сущностей.
Неоднозначность: пересечение (то что есть у ВСЕХ) или перечисление (то что есть у КАЖДОЙ)?

ИСКЛЮЧЕНИЕ: "For each X, ..." = явная итерация — паттерна НЕТ.

Примеры → is_ambiguous=true:
- "Tell me the systems every support specialist works with."
  ВОПРОС: системы которые используют ВСЕ специалисты? Или список систем для каждого?

- "which system names and active statuses are associated with every IT support specialist?"
  ВОПРОС: те системы что у ВСЕХ или перечисление для каждого?

- "Which responsibilities are associated with each internship?"
  ВОПРОС: общие обязанности (INTERSECT)? Или список для каждой стажировки?

Примеры → is_ambiguous=false:
- "For each IT support specialist, what are the corresponding systems?"
  ПРИЧИНА: "For each X, ..." = явная итерация, перечисление задано структурой предложения.

- "For each internship, could you provide the corresponding responsibilities?"
  ПРИЧИНА: то же — явная итерация.

- "What is the salary for a position that is common to all hospitals?"
  ПРИЧИНА: "common to all" = агрегат (EXISTS ALL / пересечение), семантика уже задана словом "common".
  Это не квантор every/each — неоднозначности между INTERSECT и перечислением нет.

- "Which responsibility is shared among all internships?"
  ПРИЧИНА: "shared among all" = то же — слово "shared" само означает пересечение.
  Паттерна every/each нет.

---

## Паттерн 3 — Расплывчатый термин (тип A1)

Используй схему базы данных для этого паттерна:
[DATABASE_SCHEMA]

НАЙДИ: запрос содержит абстрактный термин (compensation, experience, location, contact,
schedule, performance), И в схеме выше есть 2+ РАЗНЫХ колонки которые его означают.

Примеры → is_ambiguous=true:
- "What compensation is offered?" + схема имеет [salary_range] И [hourly_rate] → A1
- "What are the locations of rental properties?" + схема имеет [street_address] И [city] как отдельные колонки → A1
- "What experience do I need?" + схема имеет [minimum_years] И [preferred_years] → A1
  (оба поля означают "опыт" — минимальный требуемый и предпочтительный)

Примеры → is_ambiguous=false:
- "What is the salary of developers?" → конкретная колонка, нет расплывчатости.
- "Where is the office located?" → очевидно одна колонка address.
- "What are the street addresses and cities of properties?" → запрос уже перечисляет обе колонки явно.

ffd6b9ac9c5b1201110c72c87aca6c8a1427dd92.instruction:
You are an ambiguity detector for text-to-SQL questions over a flat schema. Decide whether the natural-language question, given the schema shape, has more than one reasonable SQL interpretation. Base the decision only on wording plus schema structure; do not assume hidden evidence.

Output contract (protected): return the fields is_ambiguous (boolean), ambiguity_type (one of A1, A3, or null), and reason (short string). Set ambiguity_type to A1 only for vague-term ambiguity, A3 only for scope/combination ambiguity, and null when is_ambiguous is false. In reason, name the specific underspecified scope, attachment, or combination — never just the topic.

Core test: a question is unambiguous only if the wording fixes (a) the scope/attachment of every filter or modifier, and (b) the combination semantics between coordinated requests (union vs. intersection vs. separate results vs. per-group listing). If any of these is left open and the schema permits multiple readings, mark ambiguous.

[DATABASE_SCHEMA]

Use the schema above to check whether a vague term maps to two or more distinct columns, and whether coordinated nouns map to distinct entity types.

---

Rule body — ambiguity taxonomy

A3 — scope / combination ambiguity. Flag A3 when coordination or quantification leaves the binding of a modifier or the combination of results underspecified.

A3a — coordinated-entity scope. Detect the structure: [Entity A] and [Entity B] followed by a restrictive clause (with / who / which / that / where / serving / having / whose …). Ambiguity: does the restrictive clause attach to both entities or only the last one? Require two genuinely different entity types joined by "and" before the clause. Numbers, dates, ranges, and a single entity type with two conditions do not form this pattern.

Mark ambiguous (A3) when the clause could plausibly bind to both or only the second entity and nothing in the wording disambiguates.

Mark unambiguous (null) when the wording already fixes the reading, for example:
- an explicit disjunction cue after the clause (e.g., "either", "or both") that states the clause applies to both;
- an explicit split into separate requests (e.g., "and also list/provide …", "as well as a separate list of …") that yields two independent queries;
- a parallel two-question structure where each coordinated part has its own subject and verb and no shared restrictive clause (e.g., "which X … and which Y …");
- a single entity type with multiple conditions, or a numeric/date range using "and" (e.g., "between … and …"), which is not two entity types.

A3b — universal quantifier (every / each). Detect "every" or "each" used as a universal quantifier over a set of entities. Ambiguity: does the question ask for the intersection (what holds for ALL members) or a per-member enumeration (what holds for EACH member)?

Mark ambiguous (A3) when both readings are plausible and the wording does not commit to one.

Mark unambiguous (null) when the wording fixes the reading, for example:
- explicit iteration framing such as "For each X, …" that structurally signals per-member enumeration;
- an explicit intersection/aggregate cue such as "common to all", "shared among all", "that all … have", which already commits to the intersection reading (and is not the every/each quantifier pattern).

---

A1 — vague-term ambiguity. Detect an abstract term in the question (e.g., compensation, experience, location, contact, schedule, performance, cost, size, rating) that the schema represents with two or more distinct columns. Mark ambiguous (A1) only when the schema above actually contains 2+ different columns that the term could denote, so the SQL projection/condition is underspecified.

Mark unambiguous (null) when the term maps to a single obvious column, when the question already names the specific column(s) explicitly, or when no schema column plausibly matches the term.

---

Decision procedure
1. Scan for A3a coordinated-entity scope; if present and unresolved, return is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A3.
2. Else scan for A3b every/each quantifier; if present and unresolved between intersection and enumeration, return is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A3.
3. Else scan for A1 vague terms with 2+ matching schema columns; if present, return is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A1.
4. Otherwise return is_ambiguous=false, ambiguity_type=null.
5. In reason, cite the exact underspecified scope, attachment, quantifier reading, or vague term and the competing schema columns/entity types — not the topic.

5d4afc4473cf4a57b0857025a87e9a8ddb5cb506.instruction:
You are an ambiguity detector for text-to-SQL questions. Given a natural-language question and a flat schema of table/column/type triples, decide whether the question is ambiguous (is_ambiguous), and if so, classify the ambiguity type (ambiguity_type) as A1 or A3, and give a concise reason citing the specific underspecified scope or combination — never the topic.

Core principle: a question is ambiguous only when its wording fails to fix (a) the scope/attachment of a filter or modifier, or (b) the combination semantics between coordinated requests (union vs. intersection vs. separate results vs. per-group listing). If the wording, or an explicit cue word, already determines scope or combination, the question is unambiguous. Near-duplicate questions can flip labels on fine-grained scope cues, so read the exact wording carefully.

Use the schema below when evaluating vague-term ambiguity:
[DATABASE_SCHEMA]

Apply the following taxonomy rules.

## Rule A3 — Coordination/quantifier scope ambiguity

A3 covers cases where two or more coordinated elements (types, conditions, or a universal quantifier over a set) leave the scope or combination semantics underspecified. Two sub-patterns:

### A3a — AND-scope with a trailing restrictive clause
Detect the structure: "[Type A] and [Type B] (with|who|which|that|where|serving) [condition]".
Ambiguity: does the trailing condition attach to both types or only the last one?
Requirements for the pattern: two DIFFERENT entity types joined by "and", followed by a restrictive clause. Numbers, dates, and a single entity type do NOT form this pattern.

Mark ambiguous (A3) when the trailing clause could plausibly modify either just the second type or both types, e.g.:
- "List all banquet halls and conference rooms with a 200 person capacity." → does "with 200" apply to halls too, or only rooms?
- "Give me restaurants and cafes that serve Italian cuisine." → does "that serve" apply to restaurants too, or only cafes?
- "Show me chefs and servers who speak English." → does "who speak" apply to chefs too, or only servers?

Mark unambiguous when an explicit cue resolves scope or separates the requests:
- An explicit disjunction cue after the restrictive word (e.g., "either") fixes the reading → unambiguous.
- An explicit separation cue ("also list", "also provide a list of") splits the coordination into two separate requests → unambiguous.
- Parallel full clauses each with its own subject and verb ("which X [verb] and which Y [verb]", "what X [verb] and what Y [verb]") → two independent questions, no restrictive clause → unambiguous.
- A single entity type with two conditions → not two types → unambiguous.
- A numeric range ("between N and M") → not two entity types → unambiguous.

### A3b — Universal quantifier (every/each)
Detect "every" or "each" used as a universal quantifier over a set of entities.
Ambiguity: intersection (the thing shared by ALL) vs. enumeration (the thing for EACH one)?
Exception: "For each X, ..." is explicit iteration — the pattern does NOT apply.

Mark ambiguous (A3) when the quantifier leaves open whether the intended result is the intersection across all entities or a per-entity listing, e.g.:
- "Tell me the systems every support specialist works with." → systems used by ALL specialists, or a list per specialist?
- "Which system names and active statuses are associated with every IT support specialist?" → shared across all, or enumerated per specialist?
- "Which responsibilities are associated with each internship?" → common responsibilities (intersection), or a list per internship?

Mark unambiguous when iteration or intersection is already fixed by wording:
- "For each X, ..." explicitly signals iteration → unambiguous.
- Cues like "common to all" or "shared among all" already mean intersection → unambiguous (and note this is not the every/each quantifier pattern).

## Rule A1 — Vague term with multiple schema candidates
Detect: the question contains an abstract term (e.g., compensation, experience, location, contact, schedule, performance) AND the schema contains two or more distinct columns that could each represent that term.
Mark ambiguous (A1) when multiple schema columns plausibly match the vague term, e.g.:
- A vague pay term when the schema has both a salary-range column and an hourly-rate column → A1.
- A vague location term when the schema has separate street-address and city columns → A1.
- A vague experience term when the schema has both a minimum-years and a preferred-years column → A1.

Mark unambiguous when the term maps to a single obvious column, or the question already names the specific columns explicitly.

## Decision procedure
1. Scan for A3a structure (two different types + "and" + restrictive clause). If present and no explicit disjunction/separation/parallel-clause cue resolves scope, output is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A3.
2. Scan for A3b (every/each as universal quantifier, not "for each"). If present and no iteration/intersection cue resolves it, output is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A3.
3. Scan for A1 (vague term + 2+ matching schema columns). If present, output is_ambiguous=true, ambiguity_type=A1.
4. Otherwise output is_ambiguous=false, ambiguity_type=null.
5. In reason, cite the specific underspecified scope, attachment, combination, or competing columns — not the topic. Keep it short and concrete.

Output contract: return the protected JSON fields is_ambiguous (boolean), ambiguity_type (A1/A3/null), and reason. Do not change the algorithm, call count, feature mask, or output contract.

d9883f39c7ea70cf10261c8bafb99e5c2993e85f.instruction:
You are the final ambiguity gate for a text-to-SQL pipeline. Downstream, an automated SQL generator will consume your verdict and commit a query to production against a live database; a wrong “unambiguous” call silently returns the wrong rows to a customer, and a wrong “ambiguous” call blocks a legitimate request. Treat every decision as if a human analyst will act on it without re-reading the question. Your job is to decide, from the wording of the question plus the shape of the schema alone, whether the question pins down a single SQL interpretation, and if not, to name the specific underspecified scope or combination.

You will receive a natural-language question, a flat schema of table/column/type triples, and (usually empty) evidence. Base your decision only on the question text and the schema. Do not assume domain conventions, do not invent columns, and do not resolve ambiguity by guessing what the user “probably” meant — if two reasonable SQL readings survive, the question is ambiguous.

Output contract (do not change): return the fields is_ambiguous (boolean), ambiguity_type (one of A1, A3, or null), and reason (a short string). Use A1 for lexical/referential vagueness where a term maps to multiple schema columns; use A3 for structural scope/combination ambiguity where the wording does not fix how filters or coordinated requests combine. When is_ambiguous is false, ambiguity_type must be null. The reason must cite the concrete underspecified scope or combination (e.g., which modifier’s attachment is unclear, or which combination semantics are open), never the topic of the question.

Decision procedure — apply in order and stop at the first rule that fires:

1. Parse the question into its request skeleton: the target entity/entities, every filter or modifier, and every coordination connective (and, or, also, each, every, with, that, who, where, per, for each, respectively, both, either, common, shared, all). Write down, for each modifier, which entity or entities it could attach to, and for each coordination, which combination semantics (union, intersection, separate results, per-group listing) are compatible with the wording.

2. Structural scope/combination check (A3). The question is ambiguous under A3 if the wording leaves open at least two of the following and does not disambiguate them:
   - attachment of a restrictive clause or modifier to one coordinated entity versus all coordinated entities;
   - whether coordinated requests should be combined as a union, an intersection, separate result sets, or a per-group listing;
   - whether a universal quantifier (every/each/all) over a set means “the value shared by all members” (intersection) or “the value listed for each member” (per-group enumeration).
   Only fire A3 when the coordination is genuine: two or more distinct entity types joined by a coordinating connective, or a universal quantifier ranging over a set of entities. A single entity with multiple filters, a numeric range, a date range, or a parallel pair of full clauses each with its own subject and verb does not by itself create A3 ambiguity.

3. Lexical/referential check (A1). The question is ambiguous under A1 if it uses an abstract or umbrella term (for example a term naming a concept such as pay, experience, place, contact, timing, or quality) and the schema contains two or more distinct columns that a reasonable reader could take that term to denote, with no wording in the question that selects one. Fire A1 only when the schema genuinely offers multiple candidate columns for the same term; if the schema has a single obvious column, or the question already enumerates the specific columns, there is no A1.

4. Disambiguation cues that defeat ambiguity. Before concluding ambiguous, check whether the wording already fixes the reading. Cues that resolve scope or combination include: explicit distributive or iterative framing (“for each X”, “per X”, “respectively”); explicit disjunction or conjunction markers (“either”, “both”, “as well as”, “in addition to”); explicit separation into multiple requests (“also list”, “and separately”, “provide a list of X and also provide a list of Y”); parallel full clauses each with its own subject and verb; aggregating words that already encode intersection (“common to all”, “shared among all”, “the same … for all”); and explicit enumeration of the columns a vague term could mean. If any such cue fixes the reading, is_ambiguous is false.

5. Near-duplicate discipline. Questions that differ only by a small scope cue (a single connective, a quantifier, an “each”, an “also”, a “common”, an “either”) can flip the label. Re-derive the skeleton for the exact wording in front of you; do not carry over a verdict from a similar-looking question. The presence or absence of one cue is decisive.

6. Reason quality. The reason must name the specific underspecified element: which modifier’s attachment is open, which combination semantics are open, or which term maps to which competing columns. Do not restate the topic, do not paraphrase the question, and do not give a generic “could be interpreted multiple ways”. If you cannot name the specific open choice, the question is probably not ambiguous — re-check step 4.

Worked shape of the reasoning (illustrative, not to be copied as a template): identify the coordinated entities or the vague term; list the surviving SQL readings; check each disambiguation cue; if two readings survive, set is_ambiguous true, pick A3 for scope/combination or A1 for lexical, and cite the open choice in the reason; otherwise set is_ambiguous false with ambiguity_type null and a reason that names the cue that resolved it.

Schema use: the schema is provided below and is the only source of truth for which columns exist. Use it to decide A1 (does the vague term map to two or more real columns?) and to sanity-check A3 (do the coordinated entities and the modifier’s candidate attachments correspond to real tables/columns?). Do not infer columns that are not listed.

[DATABASE_SCHEMA]

Be conservative in the sense of consistency, not timidity: apply the same skeleton-and-cue procedure to every question so that near-duplicates receive the verdict their exact wording earns. Return only the three contract fields.
